newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- FEB 14.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- FEB 14.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--A dangerous impasse has developed in Greece's schools, with teachers insisting on a fifth week of strike action and the government insisting that its purses are empty. Education Minister Gerasimos Arsenis was assertive yesterday, saying that the concessions he has made so far were being withdrawn as the strike is continuing.

--The business world came in for criticism yesterday from Prime Minister Costas Simitis for not doing their part to ensure the absorption of EU funds. The government has pledged 380 billion drachmas to the industrial investment programme, Simitis said, but absorption rates for 1996 were just 30 percent.

--US Defence Secretary Willian Cohen also raised the possibility of a clash between Greece and Turkey yesterday in Washington, following similar comments by Britain's Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind earlier in the week.

--A bill presented to Parliament yesterday foresees the extension of 2-6 month work and residency permits to Albanian citizens applying for jobs with Greek firms listed with the Greek embassy in Tirana via the Greek labour ministry.

--The leaders of Greece's opposition parties have rallied to the side of striking teachers, joining them on a night march and calling on the government to begin "substantial dialogue" with the protesters.

--Confusion over the new real estate declaration which must be submitted with 1996 tax declarations has led the finance ministry to issue a new leaflet couched in laymen's terms on how to complete the application.

--Striking teachers have achieved the impossible, uniting opposition parties in their support. At yesterday's press conference, Communist Party Secretary-General Aleka Papariga sat between conservative New Democracy president Miltiades Evert and Left Coalition leader Nikos Constantopoulos.

--Major changes to the national health system are in the pipeline, according to the latest draft of the new bill on the health system. Changes include: 24-hour access to outpatients clinics and health centres; one health body for all pension funds; and professionals to take over the economic management of hospitals and other centres.

--A final compromise on store trading hours has been worked out between traders and shop assistants: stores will close at 8pm on weekdays (9pm over summer) and 6pm on Saturdays. --Maria Petrakis, Athens Newsroom +301 3311812-4
